original_title: A Universal Intervention Program Increases Ethnic-Racial Identity Exploration and Resolution to Predict Adolescent Psychosocial Functioning One Year Later
replication_title: Out-of-school replication of the Identity Project: Randomized trial implementation and impacts on adolescent ethnic-racial identity development
replication_target_quote: This study reports on the IP's first out-of-school time replication.
outcome_quote: Results indicated that the IP led to post-intervention increases in ERI exploration and, in turn, greater ERI resolution one year later, compared to an attention control condition.
review_note: Registered RCT of the same named intervention in an out-of-school setting; exploration and later resolution reproduced. Original downstream self-esteem, depressive symptoms, and grades are not asserted here.

effect_name: Courage predicts approach despite fear
effect_claim: Courage scores predict behavioral approach among fearful people after accounting for fear severity.
effect_claim_quote: After controlling for scores on measures of spider fears, courage scores were significantly associated with approach distance to the spiders
original_title: The role of courage on behavioral approach in a fear-eliciting situation: A proof-of-concept pilot study
replication_title: The role of courage in predicting behavior: replication in a public-speaking fearful sample
replication_target_quote: This study aimed to explore the role of courage in predicting behavior.
outcome_quote: Results indicated that the CM significantly predicted speech duration after controlling for scores on a measure of public speaking fears.
review_note: Conceptual replication across feared stimuli (spiders versus speaking), using Courage Measure and behavioral approach tasks. Replica publisher references exact Norton-Weiss original DOI; same coauthor Norton.

effect_name: Anxiety and sadness shift perceived risk in opposite directions
effect_claim: Anxiety favors risk avoidance while sadness favors risk taking; in a travel decision context, anxiety should raise perceived risk relative to sadness.
effect_claim_quote: sad individuals are biased in favor of high-risk/high-reward options, whereas anxious individuals are biased in favor of low-risk/low-reward options
original_title: All Negative Moods Are Not Equal: Motivational Influences of Anxiety and Sadness on Decision Making
original_journal: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes
replication_title: The Moderating Role of Personal Relevance on Differential Priming of Anxiety and Sadness on Perceived Travel Risk: A Replication
replication_target_quote: Raghunathan and Pham conducted a pioneer study in 1999
outcome_quote: anxious participants showed higher perceived travel risk than sad participants
review_note: This is an author-described conceptual replication in travel risk perception, with the mood contrast present only at high personal relevance.

effect_name: Head Start classroom mental health prevention
effect_claim: A 12-week classroom intervention improved adaptive behavior, social interaction, and attention in Head Start children.
effect_claim_quote: significant improvements for the experimental group on adaptive behavior, social interaction, and attentional measures
original_title: Primary Prevention with Children at Risk for Emotional or Behavioral Disorders: Data on a Universal Intervention for Head Start Classrooms
replication_title: Primary Prevention in Mental Health for Head Start Classrooms: Partial Replication with Teachers as Intervenors
replication_target_quote: In a previous study, Serna, Nielsen, Lambros, and Forness (2000)
outcome_quote: Outcomes were significant on only two of eight outcome measures
review_note: The replication cites the same 2000 classroom intervention, changes intervenors to regular teachers, and finds fewer significant outcomes.

effect_name: Presentation method influences sensory suggestibility
effect_claim: Progressive increases in a suggested sensory stimulus elicited the strongest suggestibility, while progressive decreases elicited the weakest.
effect_claim_quote: Progressive Intensification of stimulation was the most successful, whereas Progressive Decrease in Intensification was least successful
original_title: The Effect of Different Types of Influence on an “Indirect-Direct” Form of a Scale of Sensory Suggestibility
replication_title: Effect of Suggestion on Perception: Replication of Gheorghiu and Reyher's Study
replication_target_quote: Gheorghiu and Reyher in 1982 described a Scale of Sensory Suggestibility
outcome_quote: Progressive Intensification and Progressive Decrease in Intensification of stimulation were the most successful
review_note: The scale was explicitly retested in a new sample; the highest method partly matched, but the originally weakest method became a strongest one.

effect_name: Personality patterns across behavioral addictions
effect_claim: Five-factor personality traits show distinct associations with different behavioral addictions.
effect_claim_quote: Conscientiousness was negatively associated with Facebook addiction, video game addiction, Internet addiction, and compulsive buying
original_title: The relationships between behavioral addictions and the five-factor model of personality
replication_title: Exploring the role of Honesty-Humility in replicating "The relationships between behavioral addictions and the five-factor model of personality"
replication_target_quote: This study is a replication of Andreassen and colleagues (2013)
outcome_quote: However, we failed to replicate the same pattern of personality traits for each behavioral addiction
review_note: The replication gives the original title and bibliographic details and reports partial support for personality associations, but a different trait pattern.

effect_name: Achievement priming improves implicit learning in novel environments
effect_claim: Priming an achievement goal improves implicit learning of the structure of a novel environment.
effect_claim_quote: two experiments, using markedly different implicit-learning paradigms, demonstrated facilitation of implicit learning when the goal of achievement was primed.
original_title: Nonconscious Goal Pursuit in Novel Environments
replication_title: No evidence for Nonconscious Goal Pursuit in Novel Environments: A Replication of Eitam et al.’s (2008) Experiment 2
replication_target_quote: we conducted a direct replication of their second experiment using materials graciously shared by the original authors.
outcome_quote: we failed to find evidence that priming of nonconscious goal pursuit facilitated implicit learning.
review_note: Direct replication of Eitam et al. 2008 Experiment 2 using original-author-shared materials. Preprint, not yet peer-reviewed; adequately powered for reported original effect but not evidence of exact zero.

effect_name: Emotion intensity shifts regulation choice toward distraction
effect_claim: High-intensity negative situations increase preference for disengagement distraction as an emotion-regulation strategy.
effect_claim_quote: in high-intensity negative situations to show a relative preference to choose to regulate emotions by disengagement distraction
original_title: Emotion-Regulation Choice
replication_title: Emotion Regulation Choice and Psychosis Proneness: A Replication and Extension Study
replication_target_quote: This study aimed to replicate and extend the results of Sheppes et al.
outcome_quote: Participants favoured disengagement strategies when the emotional intensity was high and engagement strategies when the intensity was low.
review_note: The Collabra abstract explicitly targets Sheppes et al. (2011), includes a replication task, and reports the same intensity-dependent regulation choice. The verdict addresses disengagement/distraction preference at high emotional intensity, not psychosis-proneness extension.

effect_name: Compassion predicts support for redistribution
effect_claim: People higher in dispositional compassion show stronger support for redistribution.
effect_claim_quote: Endorsement of redistribution is independently predicted by dispositional compassion
original_title: Support for redistribution is shaped by compassion, envy, and self-interest, but not a taste for fairness
original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
replication_title: Who supports redistribution? Replicating and refining effects of compassion, malicious envy, and self-interest
replication_target_quote: We conducted a close replication testing this prediction
outcome_quote: Study 1 (N = 206) confirmed the roles of self-interest (β = 0.20) and compassion for others (β = 0.37)
review_note: Publisher full text explicitly names Sznycer et al. (2017) as Study 1 target. This page isolates the compassion association, which the close replication confirmed; other envy findings are mixed.

effect_name: Second-mover advantage under negotiation information asymmetry
effect_claim: When one negotiation party knows market value and the other does not, moving second can improve the result for both parties.
effect_claim_quote: it is actually preferable for both counterparts not to give the first offer while negotiating
original_title: When your anchor sinks your boat: Information asymmetry in distributive negotiations and the disadvantage of making the first offer
replication_title: “When your anchor sinks your boat”: A replication and extension study
replication_target_quote: Maaravi and Levy (2017) recently demonstrated a second-mover advantage
outcome_quote: The second-mover advantage suggested by Maaravi and Levy was replicated
review_note: Publisher page names Maaravi and Levy (2017) Studies 3 and 4, with the exact original title and effect; the new Chinese sample reproduced the second-mover advantage, with a stated expectation boundary.

effect_name: Positive contrast after reducing bitter taste in infant rats
effect_claim: Infant rats shifted from a strongly bitter to a weakly bitter solution subsequently consumed more of the weak solution than rats always given that solution.
effect_claim_quote: the group that had been exposed to .1% quinine exhibited significantly greater intake of .01% quinine
original_title: Consummatory succesive positive contrast produced by the downshift of an aversive solution in infant rats
replication_title: Consummatory successive positive contrast with aversive solutions in infant rats: Replication and generalization to a higher concentration of a bitter solution
replication_target_quote: Recently, a similar effect was observed by lowering the concentration of a quinine solution in the experimental group.
outcome_quote: A positive successive contrast effect was evidenced by subjects in the experimental group
review_note: The publisher introduction cites the original Suárez et al. (2017b) aversive-solution experiment and the discussion explicitly says the present experiment replicates it. The original DOI was first published online in 2016 and appeared in the 2017 volume.

effect_name: Delayed rewards can lengthen rat lever presses
effect_claim: When reward requires a longer lever press, rats lengthen presses even when the reward arrives after a delay.
effect_claim_quote: This effect occurred whether reinforcers were immediate or delayed by 8 s.
original_title: Response duration is sensitive to both immediate and delayed reinforcement
original_journal: Journal of the Experimental Analysis of Behavior
replication_title: Control of response duration by delayed reinforcers: A systematic replication
replication_target_quote: Three rats responded under schedules of delayed reinforcement
outcome_quote: For all rats, response durations increased compared to those emitted under a fixed-ratio 1 schedule
review_note: The publisher introduction explicitly says it systematically replicates Byrne and Sarno (2018) and extends delay from 8 to 16 seconds. This is an experimental behavior-analysis effect in the repo Psychology slice.

effect_name: Low self-esteem and perceived safety of Facebook self-disclosure
effect_claim: People with lower self-esteem perceive Facebook disclosure as safer than face-to-face disclosure.
effect_claim_quote: We suspected that posting on Facebook would reduce the perceived riskiness of self-disclosure
original_title: When Social Networking Is Not Working
replication_title: Self-Esteem, Self-Disclosure, Self-Expression, and Connection on Facebook: A Collaborative Replication Meta-Analysis
replication_journal: Psi Chi Journal of Psychological Research
replication_target_quote: Seven pre-registered direct replication attempts of this study were conducted
outcome_quote: Self-esteem negatively predicted perceived safety of self-disclosure on Facebook as compared to face-to-face interactions (meta-analytic effect size = -.28, original effect size = -.31)
review_note: Seven preregistered direct attempts of Forest and Wood 2012 Study 1; narrow perceived-safety effect supported. Other effects in the study had mixed support.

effect_name: Negation bias for stereotype-inconsistent behavior
effect_claim: Descriptions of stereotype-inconsistent behavior use more negations than descriptions of stereotype-consistent behavior.
effect_claim_quote: people use more negations in descriptions of stereotype-inconsistent behavior than in descriptions of stereotype-consistent behavior.
original_title: The negation bias: When negations signal stereotypic expectancies.
original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
replication_title: The Negation Bias in Stereotype Maintenance: A Replication in Five Languages
replication_journal: Journal of Language and Social Psychology
replication_target_quote: a replication study of the original research conducted in Dutch (Beukeboom, Finkenauer, & Wigboldus, 2010, study 2)
outcome_quote: The results validate the existence of the Negation Bias in all five languages.
review_note: Exact Study 2 target; replicated negation bias across English, Dutch, Hungarian, Finnish, and Serbian.

effect_name: Residual risky-choice framing under matched option descriptions
effect_claim: Risky-choice framing remains when gain and loss option descriptions are matched.
effect_claim_quote: a considerable framing effect remained in our balanced design
original_title: Risky-Choice Framing Effects Result Partly From Mismatched Option Descriptions in Gains and Losses
replication_title: Risky-Choice Framing Effects Persist When Option Descriptions are Matched and Complete: A Replication and Extension of DeKay and Dou (2024)
replication_target_quote: a residual framing effect and a framing effect in choices between completely described options
outcome_quote: Risky-choice framing effects do stem partly from mismatched option descriptions, but a framing effect persists even when descriptions are matched and complete.
review_note: The preprint shares DeKay as an original author; it tests the same residual framing effect with a larger, population-matched sample and many more participants choosing between fully described options.

effect_name: Auditory rhythm shapes subsequent target detection
effect_claim: A prior rhythmic auditory signal causes rhythmic variation in later target detection accuracy.
effect_claim_quote: a low-frequency (3 Hz), amplitude-modulated signal induces a subsequent oscillation of the perceptual detectability of a brief nonperiodic acoustic stimulus
original_title: The Rhythm of Perception
replication_title:
How strong is the rhythm of perception? A registered replication of Hickok
                    et al
                    . (2015)
replication_target_quote: They tested five listeners and found that perception (target detection accuracy) fluctuated rhythmically just like the sound rhythm.
outcome_quote: Together our results strongly support the presence of oscillatory influences on target detection accuracy
review_note: Registered replication explicitly names Hickok et al. 2015 and cites exact original DOI. It reproduces rhythmic target-detection modulation in 149 listeners; this verdict does not claim an exact phase match, which the original did not show.

effect_name: Good Behavior Game reduces classroom disruption
effect_claim: Group consequences for individual rule violations reduce talking out and leaving seats in ordinary classrooms.
effect_claim_quote: The individual contingencies for the group consequences were successfully applied first during math period and then during reading period.
original_title: GOOD BEHAVIOR GAME: EFFECTS OF INDIVIDUAL CONTINGENCIES FOR GROUP CONSEQUENCES ON DISRUPTIVE BEHAVIOR IN A CLASSROOM 1
replication_title: GOOD‐BEHAVIOR GAME: A REPLICATION AND SYSTEMATIC ANALYSIS1
replication_target_quote: A good-behavior game was implemented in a fifth-grade reading class
outcome_quote: the game reduced the dependent measures from their baseline rate by almost 99% for one group and 97% for the other
review_note: The 1972 primary paper introduction explicitly attributes the Good Behavior Game to Barrish, Saunders, and Wolf (1969) and tests the same intervention with a fifth-grade class.

effect_name: Shared distress and specific anxiety and depression dimensions
effect_claim: Self-reported anxiety and depression share general distress while retaining distinct symptom dimensions.
effect_claim_quote: Specific depression and anxiety dimensions were apparent even after we controlled for negative affect.
original_title: Common and specific dimensions of self-reported anxiety and depression: Implications for the cognitive and tripartite models.
replication_title: Common and specific dimensions of self-reported anxiety and depression: A replication.
replication_target_quote: D. A. Clark, R. A. Steer, and A. T. Beck's (1994) findings
outcome_quote: the amounts of extracted variance and symptom compositions of the resultant factors were comparable to those found in the previous study
review_note: The replication abstract names the exact 1994 Clark, Steer, and Beck study and obtains comparable anxiety/depression factor structure in 1,000 outpatients.

effect_name: Care staff choose counterproductive immediate responses
effect_claim: Care staff describe psychologically appropriate long-term strategies but counterproductive immediate responses to challenging behavior.
effect_claim_quote: their immediate intervention strategies were similar to the counter-habilitative strategies
original_title: Staff strategies and explanations for intervening with challenging behaviours
replication_title: Staff strategies and explanations for intervening with challenging behaviours: a replication in a community sample
replication_target_quote: The present study replicated previous work on the beliefs of institution staff
outcome_quote: These basic findings confirmed those of previous research with institution staff
review_note: The full primary PubMed abstract names Hastings (1996) as the specific institution-staff study and reproduces the immediate/long-term response pattern in community care staff.

original_title: Susceptibility to increased high energy dense sweet and savoury food intake in response to the COVID-19 lockdown: The role of craving control and acceptance coping strategies
replication_title: Low craving control predicts increased high energy density food intake during the COVID-19 lockdown: Result replicated in an Australian sample
effect_name: Low craving control predicts increased energy-dense food intake in lockdown
effect_claim: Lower craving control predicts larger increases in high-energy-dense sweet and savoury food intake during COVID-19 lockdown.
effect_claim_quote: lower craving control was the strongest predictor of increased HED sweet and savoury food intake.
replication_target_quote: This research aimed to replicate a previous UK-based finding that low craving control predicts increased intake of high energy density foods (HED) during the COVID-19 lockdown
outcome_quote: low craving control was the only significant predictor of increased HED sweet and savoury food intake
review_note: Exact UK finding in an Australian lockdown sample. Acceptance-coping moderation did not replicate, so claim is restricted to craving-control association.

original_title: Extreme nonresponse in cognitive therapy: can behavioral activation succeed where cognitive therapy fails?
original_journal: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
replication_title: Extreme Nonresponse to Acute Phase Cognitive Therapy for Depression: An Attempt to Replicate and Extend
effect_name: Extreme nonresponse to cognitive therapy in depression
effect_claim: A sizeable subset of severely depressed patients shows extreme self-reported nonresponse to cognitive therapy, identifiable from pretreatment severity and functioning.
effect_claim_quote: a subset of patients exhibited a pattern of extreme nonresponse to cognitive therapy on self-reports of depression
replication_target_quote: we attempt a replication of the Seattle study with a larger sample of adults with recurrent MDD
outcome_quote: The rate of ENR in this large sample was only 6.3% (30/473), compared to 22.2% (10/45) in the Seattle sample.
review_note: Exact Coffman et al. 2007 target; rate markedly lower, and original predictor combination did not achieve comparable accuracy.

original_title: The moderating impact of emotional intelligence on free cortisol responses to stress
replication_title: Emotional intelligence and cortisol responses: Can laboratory findings be replicated in classrooms and using other EI measures?
effect_name: Trait emotional intelligence blunts cortisol stress response
effect_claim: Higher trait emotional intelligence predicts lower salivary cortisol response to a stressful oral presentation.
effect_claim_quote: higher trait EI scores were associated with significantly lower reactivity to stress at both psychological (i.e., mood deterioration) and biological (i.e., salivary cortisol) levels.
replication_target_quote: Laboratory studies demonstrate negative relationships between emotional intelligence (EI) and cortisol responses (Mikolajczak, Roy, Luminet, Fillee & De Timary, 2007).
outcome_quote: No significant relationships emerged between cortisol and either total EI or EI subscales
review_note: Exact original explicitly identified. Classroom group presentations and different EI measure are boundary changes; source says stress manipulation increased cortisol.

original_title: Interactive Effects of Traumatic Brain Injury and Anxiety Sensitivity Cognitive Concerns on Post-traumatic Stress Among Active Duty Soldiers
replication_title: Interactive Effects of Traumatic Brain Injury and Anxiety Sensitivity on PTSD Symptoms: A Replication and Extension in Two Clinical Samples
effect_name: Anxiety sensitivity amplifies TBI–PTSD association
effect_claim: Anxiety sensitivity cognitive concerns strengthen the association of traumatic brain injury history with post-traumatic stress symptoms.
effect_claim_quote: high ASCC potentiated the relationship between number of probable TBIs and PTS while low ASCC muted this association.
replication_target_quote: Albanese, B. J., Macatee, R. J., Schmidt, N. B., Leeson, B., Clemans, T. A., Mintz, J.,.. . Bryan, C. J. (2017b). Interactive effects of traumatic brain injury and anxiety sensitivity cognitive concerns on post-traumatic stress among active duty soldiers.
outcome_quote: Both samples revealed a significant interaction such that traumatic brain injury was more strongly linked with post-traumatic stress symptoms among those with high anxiety sensitivity cognitive concerns.
review_note: Primary Springer replication explicitly cites exact original DOI. Two clinical samples extend soldier finding.

original_title: The Dunning-Kruger effect is (mostly) a statistical artefact: Valid approaches to testing the hypothesis with individual differences data
replication_title: Reevaluating the Dunning-Kruger effect: A response to and replication of
effect_name: Minimal Dunning–Kruger nonlinearity in intelligence self-assessment
effect_claim: Valid tests of intelligence self-assessment show no substantial nonlinear Dunning–Kruger effect.
effect_claim_quote: we failed to identify statistically significant heteroscedasticity, contrary to the Dunning-Kruger hypothesis.
replication_target_quote: To address this point, recently Gignac and Zajenkowski (2020) reevaluated the DK with regards to self-assessed intelligence.
outcome_quote: our analyses illustrated a statistically significant DK effect. However, the magnitude of the effect was minimal
review_note: Exact original cited in primary ScienceDirect replication. Representative dataset and original methods found statistically detectable but tiny effect; mixed for strict null versus practical magnitude.

effect_name: Unequal parental warmth and marital distress
effect_claim: When mothers and fathers differ in whether they favor a sibling, the family shows more marital distress.
effect_claim_quote: Incongruence in differential warmth was associated with marital distress.
original_title: Congruence between Mothers' and Fathers' Differential Treatment of Siblings: Links with Family Relations and Children's Well-Being
replication_title: Family Relationships and Children's Emotional Adjustment as Correlates of Maternal and Paternal Differential Treatment: A Replication with Toddler and Preschool Siblings
replication_target_quote: This study attempted to replicate the findings of McHale, Crouter, McGuire, and Updegraff
outcome_quote: Incongruent patterns of differential favoritism (i.e., one parent treats the children equally while the other favors one child) were associated with marital distress.
review_note: The replication names the exact McHale et al. original and tests the same family-level incongruence and marital distress relationship with younger siblings; other developmental findings differ.

effect_name: Self-determined death reminders do not increase worldview defense
effect_claim: Death reminders increased ingroup or worldview defense only when death was framed as outside personal control.
effect_claim_quote: WD was only increased following pure death salience, compared with both dental pain salience and salience of self-determined death.
original_title: The role of control motivation in mortality salience effects on ingroup support and defense.
original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
replication_title: The Possibility of Self-Determined Death Eliminates Mortality Salience Effects on Cultural Worldview Defense: Cross-Cultural Replications
replication_target_quote: self-determined dying (i.e., controllable death) does not (Fritsche, Jonas, & Fankhänel, 2008)
outcome_quote: rep-licated the effect in both a highly individualistic culture
review_note: The 2016 primary publisher abstract explicitly identifies Fritsche, Jonas, and Fankhänel (2008) and reports reproducing the uncontrollable-versus-self-determined death effect in US and Chinese samples.

effect_name: Beliefs about nightmares predict distress beyond nightmare frequency
effect_claim: Stronger beliefs about nightmares were associated with greater nightmare distress even after accounting for nightmare frequency.
effect_claim_quote: The beliefs about nightmares scale contributed to nightmare distress independently from nightmare frequency.
original_title: Nightmare distress, nightmare frequency, and beliefs about nightmares
replication_title: Nightmare Distress, Beliefs About Nightmares, and Personality: A Research Note and Replication
replication_target_quote: The present study aimed at replicating previously reported relationships between gender, neuroticism, beliefs about nightmares, nightmare frequency, and nightmare distress in an independent sample.
outcome_quote: The findings of the present study indicated–as expected–that beliefs about nightmares, gender, and neuroticism contribute independently to nightmare distress–in addition to nightmare frequency.

effect_name: Pigeons prefer an unsegmented reward interval
effect_claim: Pigeons preferred a simple unsegmented reinforcement schedule over a segmented chained schedule of equal total duration.
effect_claim_quote: With few exceptions, the simple schedule was preferred to the chained schedule.
original_title: PREFERENCE FOR SIMPLE INTERVAL SCHEDULES OF REINFORCEMENT IN CONCURRENT CHAINS: EFFECTS OF SEGMENTATION RATIO
original_journal: Journal of the Experimental Analysis of Behavior
replication_title: PSYCHOLOGICAL DISTANCE TO REWARD: A HUMAN REPLICATION
replication_journal: Journal of the Experimental Analysis of Behavior
replication_target_quote: In the terminal link, the appearance of an enemy aircraft was determined by a pair of differentially segmented fixed-time schedules (Experiment 1) or fixed-interval schedules (Experiment 2) of equal overall duration.
outcome_quote: subjects preferred the unsegmented to the segmented intervals.

effect_name: Effort moralization independent of outcome
effect_claim: People judge greater effort as more morally admirable even when it does not improve an outcome.
effect_claim_quote: The exertion of effort is deemed morally admirable (Studies 1-6)
original_title: The moralization of effort
replication_title: Is It Worth the Hustle? A Multi-Country Replication of the Effort Moralization Effect and an Extension to Generational Differences in the Appreciation of Effort
replication_target_quote: We replicated this effect, based on Celniker et al. (2023, Study 6)
outcome_quote: Our findings support the generalizability of effort moralization to Germany and Mexico
review_note: Exact Celniker Study 6 replication in Germany and Mexico; registered report. Age-extension null is separate.

effect_name: Physiological arousal increases information sharing
effect_claim: Incidental physiological arousal increases willingness to share information.
effect_claim_quote: Arousal boosted sharing of information.
original_title: Arousal Increases Social Transmission of Information
replication_title: Does Physiological Arousal Increase Social Transmission of Information? Two Replications of Berger (2011)
replication_target_quote: We conducted two replications
outcome_quote: Both studies failed to find an impact of incidental physiological arousal on undergraduate participants' willingness to share news articles on social media.
review_note: Correct original Berger 2011 DOI, replacing wrong machine link to Can Losing Lead to Winning? Same arousal manipulation; email original versus social-media sharing replication. Two preregistered studies.

effect_name: Vegetative patients perceived as having less mind than the dead
effect_claim: People attribute less mental capacity to patients in a persistent vegetative state than to dead people.
effect_claim_quote: Experiment 1 found that PVS patients were perceived to have less mental capacity than the dead.
original_title: More dead than dead: Perceptions of persons in the persistent vegetative state
replication_title: The living dead? Perception of persons in the unresponsive wakefulness syndrome in Germany compared to the USA
replication_target_quote: A previous US-American study indicated that participants ascribed even less mind to patients with unresponsive-wakefulness-syndrome (UWS) than to the dead.
outcome_quote: Unlike the US sample, German participants did not perceive UWS patients as "more dead than dead"
review_note: Correct original Gray et al. 2011 DOI, replacing wrong objectification paper; direct Germany-versus-US comparison. Cultural boundary noted.

effect_name: Trait-based antisocial personality model predicts psychopathy
effect_claim: DSM-5 Section III trait-based antisocial personality disorder criteria predict psychopathy better than Section II categorical criteria.
effect_claim_quote: Analyses showed that Section III ASPD outperformed Section II ASPD in predicting scores on Hare's (2003) Psychopathy Checklist-Revised (PCL-R; r = .88 vs. .59).
original_title: Examining the DSM–5 alternative personality disorder model operationalization of antisocial personality disorder and psychopathy in a male correctional sample.
original_journal: Personality Disorders: Theory, Research, and Treatment
replication_title: Psychopathy and antisocial personality disorder in the fifth edition of the American Psychiatric Association’s Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders: An attempted replication of Wygant et al. (2016).
replication_journal: Personality Disorders: Theory, Research, and Treatment
replication_target_quote: Wygant et al. found that the DSM-5 Section III AMPD outperformed Section II in predicting various operationalizations of psychopathy in a sample of 200 male inmates.
outcome_quote: Analyses showed a partial replication of Wygant et al.'s findings
review_note: Exact Wygant et al. original and AMPD versus Section II target. Abstract reports partial replication, without effect-size details; mixed verdict reflects authors' characterization.

effect_name: Comfort food buffers loneliness after a belongingness threat
effect_claim: For securely attached people, thinking about comfort food after a belongingness threat reduces loneliness.
effect_claim_quote: comfort foods buffer against belongingness threats in people who already have positive associations with relationships (i.e., are secure in attachment style)
original_title: Chicken Soup Really Is Good for the Soul
replication_title: Is Comfort Food Really Good for the Soul? A Replication of Troisi and Gabriel’s (2011) Study 2
replication_target_quote: three high-powered replications of Troisi and Gabriel’s (2011) idea that writing about comfort food reduces feelings of loneliness amongst securely attached individuals after a belongingness threat
outcome_quote: We did not confirm the overall effect over all three countries.
review_note: The replication title explicitly identifies Troisi and Gabriel (2011) Study 2; the abstract tests the same secure-attachment comfort-food buffer across three samples (total N=649). Its abstract reports no overall effect.

effect_name: A lucky golf ball improves putting performance
effect_claim: Activating a good-luck superstition by giving participants a lucky golf ball improves golf performance.
effect_claim_quote: activating good-luck-related superstitions via a common saying or action (e.g., "break a leg," keeping one's fingers crossed) or a lucky charm improves subsequent performance in golfing
original_title: Keep Your Fingers Crossed!
replication_title: Replication of the Superstition and Performance Study by
replication_target_quote: examining if telling participants they had a lucky golf ball could improve their performance on a 10-shot golf task relative to controls
outcome_quote: Participants told they had a lucky ball performed almost identically to controls.
review_note: Crossref metadata for DOI 10.1027/1864-9335/a000190 identifies Calin-Jageman and Caldwell (2014), a published two-study replication of Damisch et al. (2010). Its primary abstract names the precise lucky-golf-ball intervention and reports essentially identical performance. The OSF project links the same published article.

effect_name: Beliefs about motivation fit eager and vigilant tasks
effect_claim: American participants expect promotion-focused thinking to help eager tasks and prevention-focused thinking to help vigilant tasks when task outcomes concern themselves.
effect_claim_quote: Westerners only recognized how to do so for independent outcomes.
original_title: A Cross-Cultural Investigation of Metamotivational Beliefs About Regulatory Focus Task-Motivation Fit
replication_title: Metamotivational Beliefs about Promotion and Prevention Focus: Replications of the American-Independent Conditions of Nguyen et al.’s (2021) Studies 2 and 3
replication_target_quote: This research replicated two pre-pandemic experiments
outcome_quote: Effect sizes tended to be large and were in the same directions and slightly larger than in the original experiments.
review_note: The OSF title identifies Nguyen et al. (2021) Studies 2 and 3, American-independent conditions. Its wiki reports the same promotion/eager and prevention/vigilant belief pattern. The original abstract reports Westerners recognize fit for independent outcomes.

effect_name: Neighborhood composition weakens minority contact benefits
effect_claim: For minority group members, contact with the majority group reduces prejudice less in majority-dense neighborhoods than in minority-dense neighborhoods.
effect_claim_quote: This relationship, however, was weak or non-existent when they lived in primarily European neighborhoods.
original_title: The wallpaper effect: the contact hypothesis fails for minority group members who live in areas with a high proportion of majority group members
replication_title: The “Wallpaper Effect” Revisited: Divergent Findings on the Effects of Intergroup Contact on Attitudes in Diverse Versus Nondiverse Contexts
replication_target_quote: This article reexamines the so-called "wallpaper effect" of intergroup contact
outcome_quote: Results failed to replicate the previously reported findings
review_note: The later paper explicitly identifies Barlow et al. (2013) as the original wallpaper-effect study (Oxford primary manuscript). Five studies tested the same moderation of contact benefits by outgroup neighborhood share and largely found null interactions. Corrected the packet proposed Putnam 2007 link, which is background only.

effect_name: Words activate concepts faster than associated sounds
effect_claim: Spoken object labels facilitate identification of matching visual objects more than associated nonverbal sounds.
effect_claim_quote: verbal cues, such as the word "cat," lead to faster and more accurate verification of congruent objects
original_title: The evocative power of words: activation of concepts by verbal and nonverbal means
replication_title: Infants’ conceptual representations of meaningful verbal and nonverbal sounds
replication_target_quote: We aimed to replicate these findings and extend them to infants.
outcome_quote: adults reacted faster when the visual object matched the auditory stimulus and even faster in the word relative to the associated sound condition
review_note: The 2020 paper full text explicitly says Experiment 1A replicated Lupyan and Thompson-Schill (2012) in adults using a similar visual identification task. Original primary abstract reports label advantage over associated sounds. The packet proposed a different crossmodal study.

effect_name: Consensus messages increase reactance among climate-skeptical Republicans
effect_claim: Emphasizing the scientific consensus increased psychological reactance among Republicans who questioned whether climate change exists.
effect_claim_quote: adding political identification to the model as an additional moderating variable shows the increases in reactance occur among Republicans who question the existence of climate change.
original_title: Psychological Reactance From Reading Basic Facts on Climate Change: The Role of Prior Views and Political Identification
replication_title: Exposure to Scientific Consensus Does Not Cause Psychological Reactance
replication_target_quote: They find no main effect of the consensus message on psychological reactance, but a subsequent moderation analysis appears to show reactance among audiences who question the existence of climate change, especially Republicans. Here we attempt to replicate this finding
outcome_quote: However, in contrast to Ma et al., we find no evidence of psychological reactance among Republicans, conservatives, or those with dismissive prior views.
review_note: Corrected original DOI: candidate linked a different Dixon study. Later paper explicitly names Ma, Dixon & Hmielowski (2019); publisher abstracts and earlier online publication date (2018-12-27) were verified at Taylor & Francis.

effect_name: Fructose or glucose ingestion improves anagram performance
effect_claim: Consuming fructose or glucose before the task increased the number of anagrams solved relative to placebo.
effect_claim_quote: It was observed that consuming fructose and glucose resulted in the resolution of more anagrams than the placebo.
original_title: Can you enhance executive control without glucose? The effects of fructose on problem solving
replication_title: What Enables Self-Control? A Test of Glucose, Fructose, and Vagus Nerve Activation as Possible Factors
replication_target_quote: This study replicated the study by Miller, Bourrasseau, and Blampain (2013) on the effects of fructose and glucose on self-control.
outcome_quote: In contrast to the results obtained by Miller et al. (2013), it was found that fructose, glucose, and VM did not increase the participants' levels of self-control compared to control subjects.
review_note: Corrected original DOI from wrong organizational-routines Miller paper. Later primary journal page cites exact Miller, Bourrasseau, and Blampain 2013 DOI in references; original abstract is publisher-submitted Crossref.

effect_name: Delayed production reduces disruption of perceptual learning
effect_claim: Delaying production after hearing a speech sound reduced or eliminated the disruption of perceptual learning caused by immediate production.
effect_claim_quote: Increasing the delay between perception and production on a trial can reduce and even eliminate disruption of perceptual learning.
original_title: Just give it time: Differential effects of disruption and delay on perceptual learning
replication_title: Wait long and prosper! Delaying production alleviates its detrimental effect on word learning
replication_target_quote: Recent work by Baese-Berk and Samuel (Baese-Berk, M. M., & Samuel, A. G. (2022). Just give it time: Differential effects of disruption and delay on perceptual learning. Attention, Perception, & Psychophysics, 84(3), 960–980.) suggests that immediate – but not delayed – production has a detrimental effect on learning a non-native speech sound contrast. We tested whether this pattern is also found for word learning.
outcome_quote: Critically, in line with our prediction, this negative effect disappeared when a 4-second pause was inserted between hearing and producing each word.
review_note: Corrected original DOI from unrelated Samuel & Dumay paper. Conceptual replication/extension from non-native sound contrast to word learning, with the exact Baese-Berk & Samuel 2022 study named in the later publisher abstract. Both journal publisher abstracts verified; March original predates November later article.

effect_name: Current thirst colors judgments of others’ thirst
effect_claim: People made thirsty themselves rate thirst as more bothersome for other people who lack food and water.
effect_claim_quote: participants' predictions of whether thirst or hunger would be more bothersome to hikers lost without food or water were biased in the direction of participants' own exercise-induced thirst
original_title: Social projection of transient drive states
replication_title: More Than Skin Deep
replication_target_quote: Van Boven & Loewenstein, 2003
outcome_quote: participants who ate salty snacks without water thought other people were overly bothered by thirst (Study 2)
review_note: The 2012 primary full text explicitly adapts the hiker story from Van Boven and Loewenstein (2003). It repeats the thirst-projection effect for similar others but reports that the effect evaporated for people with opposed political views, so outcome is mixed. Corrects an unrelated visceral-fit DOI proposed by the discovery link.

effect_name: Cultural identity priming shifts autobiographical memory focus
effect_claim: Priming Asian American participants with their American rather than Asian identity increased self-focused and reduced socially oriented autobiographical memories.
effect_claim_quote: Those whose American self was activated recalled more self-focused and less socially oriented memories than those whose Asian self was made salient, with the control group falling in between.
original_title: Being American, being Asian: The bicultural self and autobiographical memory in Asian Americans
replication_title: Biculturals’ Flexible Identity Affects the Retrieval of Autobiographical Memories: an Online Replication of Wang (2008) Using a Pretest-Posttest Group Design
replication_target_quote: The current study is a conceptual replication of Wang (2008) using a pretest-posttest design and an online sample through Amazon’s Mechanical Turk.
outcome_quote: However, on post-prime memories, participants primed as American recalled more self-focused memories than relationally focused memories and those primed as Asian recalled more relationally focused memories than self-focused memories.
review_note: Corrected original DOI from unrelated Wang and Dvorak Sweet Future. Later title and publisher-submitted Crossref abstract explicitly identify Wang 2008 and report six of eight replicated effects; original publisher abstract is indexed in PubMed. Conceptual replication with online pretest-posttest sample.

effect_name: Early pseudoword familiarization gives concordant recognition rates
effect_claim: With little familiarization, higher-frequency pseudowords yield increases in both recognition hits and false alarms rather than a classic mirror effect.
effect_claim_quote: both hits and false alarms on recognition tests increased as a function of prior frequency
original_title: Direct and indirect stimulus-frequency effects in recognition.
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
replication_title: A reexamination of stimulus-frequency effects in recognition: Two mirrors for low- and high-frequency pseudowords.
replication_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
replication_target_quote: Recognition tests given during the first week of familiarization replicated a result of W. T. Maddox and W. K. Estes (1997)
outcome_quote: failed to show the classic word-frequency mirror effect for pseudowords
review_note: Initial-week result replicated; later extended training produced the mirror pattern. Claim restricted to low familiarization.

effect_name: Context change makes prior remembering forgettable
effect_claim: Changing the context of a recalled item makes people less likely to remember having recalled it before.
effect_claim_quote: Participants more often forgot that they had previously recalled an item if they were cued to think of it differently on the two tests.
original_title: Remembering remembering.
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
replication_title: Replicating remembering “remembering”
replication_target_quote: we aimed to replicate the third experiment of Arnold and Lindsay (2002) using the same neutral context sentences.
outcome_quote: The effect was replicated by using the same neutral context sentences
review_note: Corrects wrong machine original Abenavoli & Henkel 2008. Primary replication paper explicitly identifies Arnold & Lindsay 2002 Experiment 3 in its methods and credits original author materials.

effect_name: Syntactic category limits lexical competition
effect_claim: During sentence production, semantically related words compete for selection within a syntactic category but not across noun–verb categories.
effect_claim_quote: nouns (e.g., running as a noun) do not compete with verbs (e.g., walking as a verb) and verbs do not compete with nouns in sentence production
original_title: Syntactic category constrains lexical competition in speaking.
replication_title: Semantic interference across word classes during lexical selection in Dutch
replication_target_quote: Momma, Buffinton, Slevc, and Phillips (2020, Cognition) showed experimentally that word class indeed constrains lexical selection.
outcome_quote: In two experiments, we found a semantic interference effect, but, contrary to the original study, no evidence for a word class constraint.
review_note: Corrects wrong machine original Mahon et al. 2007. Conceptual replication in Dutch; language change may explain boundary.

effect_name: Comorbid OCD and PTSD increases OCD symptom severity
effect_claim: People with both OCD and PTSD report more severe OCD symptoms than people with OCD alone, while PTSD severity is similar to PTSD alone.
effect_claim_quote: Individuals who exceeded cutoffs for probable OCD + PTSD endorse more severe OCD symptoms overall but report similar levels of PTSD symptoms compared with the respective diagnostic groups.
original_title: Common Symptom Presentations in Individuals With Probable Comorbid Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder and Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
original_journal: The Journal of Nervous and Mental Disease
replication_title: Symptom severity and presentation in comorbid OCD and PTSD: A clinical replication
replication_target_quote: only one study to date has examined typical OCD and PTSD presentations in individuals with OCD+PTSD, and findings were based on a nonclinical sample
outcome_quote: patients with OCD+PTSD reported more severe OCD yet similar severity PTSD symptoms
review_note: The later paper explicitly states it clinically replicates the only previous nonclinical OCD+PTSD symptom-presentation study. Its publisher reference list cites Pinciotti and Orcutt (2020), DOI 10.1097/NMD.0000000000001211. The earlier study sampled 133 undergraduates; the later study sampled 1,014 clinical patients and reproduced the same severity pattern. Corrected unrelated Foa review link.

effect_name: Opposite-offset training disrupts visual hyperacuity learning
effect_claim: Training on an opposite-offset visual hyperacuity task immediately after the first task disrupted learning of the first task at the same retinotopic location.
effect_claim_quote: We first show that disruption of learning occurs between visual stimuli presented at the same orientation in the same retinotopic location but not for the same stimuli presented at retinotopically disparate locations or different orientations at the same location.
original_title: Task-specific disruption of perceptual learning
original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
replication_title: Retrograde Interference in Perceptual Learning of a Peripheral Hyperacuity Task
replication_target_quote: To address this controversy, we decided to replicate our initial finding of retrograde interference for 3-dot hyperacuity.
outcome_quote: We find that retrograde interference occurs when eye-movements are tightly controlled, using a gaze-contingent display, where the peripheral stimuli were only presented when subjects maintained fixation. On the other hand, no retrograde interference was found in a group of subjects who performed the task without this fixation control.
review_note: Corrected original DOI from Aberg & Herzog 2010 null-result paper: later article explicitly says it replicated its own Seitz et al. 2005 3-dot hyperacuity finding, with Aberg & Herzog as the intervening contrary report. Effect recurs only with gaze-contingent fixation control; no effect without it, hence mixed. Human behavioral perceptual-learning study from psychology department.

effect_name: Romantic partners imitate observed goal disengagement
effect_claim: Adults who watched a romantic partner disengage from an unsolvable puzzle switched puzzles more often than control participants.
effect_claim_quote: Adults in the GE group switched significantly less than in the GD or CO group, whereas subjects in the GD group switched significantly more often than the CO group.
original_title: Modelling goal adjustment in social relationships: Two experimental studies with children and adults
replication_title: Imitation of Goal Engagement and Disengagement Processes in Romantic Relationships
replication_target_quote: First, it set out to replicate the modelling effect obtained in Thomsen et al. (2017), that is, whether observing a partner coping with obstacles in goal pursuit influences the observer's behaviour in the same task.
outcome_quote: Observers in the disengagement group (M = 4.71, SD = 1.40) switched significantly more often than participants in the control group (M = 3.82, SD = 1.34), mean difference = 0.88, BCa 95% CI [0.16, 1.58], d = 0.65.
review_note: Corrected original DOI from Wrosch et al. 2003 conceptual article. Later primary publisher full text explicitly identifies Thomsen et al. 2017, DOI in reference list, and says it mirrored the 2017 paradigm. Original author abstract from Crossref reports adult group direction. Original first published online October 2016, print 2017.

effect_name: Gelotophobia correlates with anxious and avoidant romantic attachment
effect_claim: Greater fear of being laughed at is associated with greater anxious and avoidant romantic attachment.
effect_claim_quote: gelotophobia goes along with higher expressions in attachment anxiety and avoidance
original_title: Extending the Study of Gelotophobia, Gelotophilia, and Katagelasticism in Romantic Life Toward Romantic Attachment
replication_title: Gelotophobia in romantic life: Replicating associations with attachment styles and their mediating role for relationship status
replication_journal: Journal of Social and Personal Relationships
replication_target_quote: This study aims to replicate (a) the associations between gelotophobia and romantic attachment
outcome_quote: gelotophobia positively relates to avoidant and anxious attachment
review_note: Corrected wrong machine original DOI. Sage publisher abstract and reference identify Brauer, Proyer & Ruch DOI 10.1027/1614-0001/a000307. Independent later N=531 sample. Crossref original publication date is April 2020 at month precision, represented conservatively here by April 30 as latest possible day; replication publisher confirms July 23, 2020. Association replicated, but avoidance mediation did not, so claim is restricted to attachment associations.

effect_name: Cookie cues increase high risk choices
effect_claim: When the chance of losing lab time is high, seeing and smelling cookies increases willingness to play for them.
effect_claim_quote: were almost twice as likely to play the high-risk game than were participants in the non-visceral condition
original_title: Visceral influences on risk‐taking behavior
replication_title: An appetite for risk? Failure to replicate the effect of hunger cues on risk taking
replication_target_quote: We attempted to replicate this specific contrast in two studies.
outcome_quote: we failed to observe a main effect of exposure to external food cues on risk-taking.
review_note: The Festjens manuscript identifies Ditto et al. as its target and reproduces the cookie risk task, focusing on the high-loss-probability contrast. Its abstract says Ditto (1996), but its full discussion and publisher article correctly identify Ditto et al. (2006), DOI 10.1002/bdm.520. Original author-hosted full text reports near doubling of high-risk game choices with visible/smellable cookies; later two-study manuscript reports no main cue effect. Corrects wrong discovery link to self-control risk perception.

effect_name: Climate consensus messages shift beliefs and support for action
effect_claim: Increasing perceived scientific consensus on human-caused climate change increased climate beliefs and worry, which predicted greater support for public action.
effect_claim_quote: Using national data (N = 1104) from a consensus-message experiment, we find that increasing public perceptions of the scientific consensus is significantly and causally associated with an increase in the belief that climate change is happening, human-caused and a worrisome threat. In turn, changes in these key beliefs are predictive of increased support for public action.
original_title: The Scientific Consensus on Climate Change as a Gateway Belief: Experimental Evidence
replication_title: The gateway belief model: A large-scale replication
replication_target_quote: The main objective of the present study is to provide a confirmatory replication of the Gateway Belief Model (GBM) by van der Linden et al. (2015b).
outcome_quote: Results support the mediational hypotheses of the GBM: an experimentally induced change in perceived scientific consensus causes subsequent changes in cognitive (belief) and affective (worry) judgments about climate change, which in turn are associated with changes in support for public action.
review_note: Corrected original DOI from a GM-food gateway-belief study. Later Elsevier full text explicitly identifies van der Linden et al. 2015b as direct confirmatory original, and author manuscript at Cambridge repository has exact outcome abstract. Original PLOS article has the same climate consensus message and mediational belief/action claim.

effect_name: Saying “I am excited” improves public speaking
effect_claim: Before public speaking, reappraising anxiety as excitement improves observed speaking performance compared with trying to calm down.
effect_claim_quote: Compared with those who attempt to calm down, individuals who reappraise their anxious arousal as excitement feel more excited and perform better.
original_title: Get excited: reappraising pre-performance anxiety as excitement
replication_title: Getting Excited About Public Speaking: A Replication
replication_target_quote: Brooks (2014, Study 2) predicted and found that college students who were instructed to say aloud
outcome_quote: no differences between conditions on any observer ratings of performance
review_note: The later paper explicitly identifies Brooks (2014) Study 2 and the same “I am excited” versus “I am calm” speech task. The original reported better performance; the replication reproduced self-report excitement but not observer-rated speech performance. Effect-specific outcome is failed.

effect_name: Shared language makes infants expect affiliation
effect_claim: Infants expect two people who speak the same language to affiliate more than two people who speak different languages.
effect_claim_quote: Results suggest that infants expected two people who spoke the same language to be more likely to affiliate than two people who spoke different languages.
original_title: Preverbal Infants Infer Third-Party Social Relationships Based on Language
replication_title: Will They Get Along? An Online Replication of Infants' Expectations about Third Party Social Relationships Based on Language
replication_target_quote: This study is a replication of a 2017 study "Preverbal Infants Infer Third-Party Social Relationships Based on Language" by Liberman, Woodward, and Kinzler
outcome_quote: Results from this study showed no significant differences in infants' expectations based on the language of the speakers.
review_note: The 2021 University of Chicago thesis names Liberman, Woodward, and Kinzler (2017) and reproduces the same shared-versus-different language affiliation video paradigm online. It reports no difference in infant expectations.

effect_name: Objective status lowers system justification in China
effect_claim: In China, higher objective socioeconomic status predicts less justification of the social system.
effect_claim_quote: objective SES is more related to access to information about the social reality, which may increase criticism about the system and lead to lower system justification.
original_title: Testing the Status-Legitimacy Hypothesis in China: Objective and Subjective Socioeconomic Status Divergently Predict System Justification
replication_title: Testing the status‐legitimacy hypothesis: Predicting system justification using objective and subjective socioeconomic status in China and the United States
replication_target_quote: Li, Yang, Wu, and Kou (2020, Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin)
outcome_quote: we failed to replicate Li et al.'s findings surrounding objective SES in China during cross‐sectional and cross‐lagged analyses.
review_note: The later paper names Li, Yang, Wu, and Kou (2020) and repeats objective/subjective SES prediction in China and the US. Its abstract says subjective SES replicated but the original negative objective-SES association did not replicate in China. This row is specific to the latter effect.

effect_name: Uncontrollable evaluative-conditioning influence persists under reversal instructions
effect_claim: An affective stimulus influenced evaluations of paired neutral stimuli even when participants were instructed to reverse that influence; modelling found an uncontrollable component.
effect_claim_quote: the experiment also yielded evidence for uncontrollable EC effects reflected by a significant u-parameter that captures evaluations in line with US valence irrespective of instructions.
original_title: Dissociating Controllable and Uncontrollable Effects of Affective Stimuli on Attitudes and Consumption
replication_title: Evidence suggestive of uncontrollable attitude acquisition replicates in an instructions-based evaluative conditioning paradigm: Implications for associative attitude acquisition
replication_target_quote: To date, the most convincing support for uncontrollable attitude formation stems from evaluative conditioning (EC) studies by Hütter and Sweldens (2018).
outcome_quote: Fully replicating effects found in the standard (i.e., experienced) EC paradigm, (i) the absolute EC effect was larger in the standard than reversed learning condition, and (ii) outcomes from Multinomial Processing Tree modelling suggested both controllable and uncontrollable EC effects.
review_note: Corrected original DOI from De Houwer et al. 2012, which tested EC without direct experienced pairing but not the uncontrollable component. Later author manuscript explicitly cites Hütter & Sweldens 2018 and adapts its Experiment 4, then reports an uncontrollable u-parameter in the instruction-only conceptual replication. Original quote is from published-paper PDF in Erasmus University repository; later abstract and DOI from author university repository.

effect_name: Low status animalization and high status mechanization
effect_claim: People attribute more animal-like qualities to low socioeconomic status groups and more machine-like qualities to high status groups.
effect_claim_quote: the low-SES group was animalized in comparison with the high-SES group, which was mechanized
original_title: Animalizing the disadvantaged, mechanizing the wealthy: The convergence of socio-economic status and attribution of humanity
replication_title: Dehumanization and Socioeconomic Status: Replicating and Extending the Animalization of Low-SES Targets and the Mechanization of High-SES Targets
replication_target_quote: replicated Sainz et al.’s first study
outcome_quote: confirming the animalization of low-SES groups but not consistently supporting the mechanization of high-SES groups
review_note: Corrected wrong machine original DOI. Sage publisher abstract explicitly names Sainz et al. Study 1 and references the exact 2019 original DOI. Study 1 reproduces animalization but not consistent mechanization; adapted Study 2 and extended Study 3 support both. Mixed for this joint claim, not a blanket failure.

effect_name: Dog portraits favor the left cheek
effect_claim: Photographs of dogs are more likely to show their left cheek than their right cheek.
effect_claim_quote: We observed significant leftward biases in photographs of infants and non-human animals.
original_title: Photographer preference or image purpose? An investigation of posing bias in mammalian and non-mammalian species
replication_title: NO CHEEK BIAS FOR NON-PRIMATES: AN INSTAGRAM REPLICATION OF THOMAS ET AL. (2006)
replication_target_quote: Thomas et al.’s (2006) finding of a left cheek bias for dogs
outcome_quote: there were no cheek biases for images of nonhuman animals (dogs, cats, lizards, fish)
review_note: The later paper explicitly names Thomas et al. (2006) and the original dog-left-cheek result. The correct original is Thomas, Burkitt, and Saucier (2006) DOI 10.1080/13576500600623983, whose primary abstract reports leftward biases for nonhuman animal photographs. The larger Instagram study found no dog bias; it did find a left-cheek bias for human infants, so this row is effect-specific to dogs.

effect_name: Negative emotion differentiation buffers rumination related self injury
effect_claim: For people with borderline personality disorder, rumination predicts more self injury chiefly when they struggle to distinguish negative emotions.
effect_claim_quote: A significant rumination by negative emotion differentiation interaction revealed that rumination predicted higher rates of NSSI acts and urges in participants with difficulty differentiating their negative emotions.
original_title: Emotion differentiation as a protective factor against nonsuicidal self-injury in borderline personality disorder
original_authors: Zaki, Coifman, Rafaeli, Berenson, and Downey
replication_title: Emotion Differentiation as a Protective Factor Against the Behavioral Consequences of Rumination: A Conceptual Replication and Extension in the Context of Social Anxiety
replication_target_quote: the present investigation sought to replicate and extend Zaki et al. (2013)’s findings in the context of SAD.
outcome_quote: NED significantly moderated the relationship between rumination and social avoidance such that the positive association between rumination and social avoidance remained significant only for low NED.
review_note: Explicit conceptual replication and extension: the later paper tests the protective negative-emotion-differentiation by rumination interaction in social anxiety and social avoidance, rather than repeating the original borderline personality disorder and self-injury outcome. Linked PDF is the author thesis underlying the published article.

effect_name: Four personality profiles mark clinical differences in adolescents with disruptive behavior disorders
effect_claim: Adolescents with disruptive behavior disorders form four distinct personality profiles that differ in clinical functioning.
effect_claim_quote: Four distinct personality types ("disinhibited," "high distress," "low distress," "positive") were meaningfully different from one another.
original_title: Personality Heterogeneity in Adolescents With Disruptive Behavior Disorders
replication_title: Personality heterogeneity in adolescents with disruptive behavior disorders: A conceptual replication study
replication_authors: Rivard, Le Corff, Déry, Bégin, and Lapalme
replication_target_quote: This registered report is a conceptual replication of the study conducted by Wilson, Hopwood, McGue, and Iacono (2019)
outcome_quote: Latent profile analyses using parent- and adolescent-reported the Big Five domains revealed two- and three-profile solutions, respectively. When controlling for sex, results from the manual BCH method for auxiliary variables showed that profile membership is associated with different clinically relevant outcomes, such as comorbid psychological disorders, risky sexual behavior, and attachment to parents and friends.
review_note: The registered conceptual replication found clinically differentiated personality profiles but two parent-rated and three adolescent-rated profiles, rather than the original four. Mixed is for the joint four-profile and clinical-differentiation claim. Author accepted manuscript is primary source.

effect_name: Personality disorder label does not shift diminished responsibility verdicts
effect_claim: A personality disorder diagnostic label in a mock homicide trial did not change jurors’ decisions on diminished responsibility.
effect_claim_quote: Between-group differences in other measures, including the decision to agree a verdict of diminished responsibility, were not found
original_title: Juror decision-making regarding a defendant diagnosed with Borderline Personality Disorder
replication_title: Juror Decision-Making and Diminished Responsibility: Diagnosis Has Little Impact, but Stigma May Matter (A Partial Replication of Baker et al. (2022))
replication_journal: Journal of Forensic Psychology Research and Practice
replication_target_quote: partially replicate previous research which had investigated how a personality disorder diagnosis may influence juror decision-making concerning the partial defence of Diminished Responsibility
outcome_quote: diagnostic manipulation made little difference to Diminished Responsibility decisions
review_note: Corrected wrong machine original DOI. Replica title names Baker et al. (2022), coauthors overlap, original and later experiments both compare a personality disorder label with a complex mental health description in mock homicide trials. Both found no diagnostic-label effect on diminished responsibility verdicts. Partial replication with altered label variants and online video vignettes; original danger/segregation attitudes are not included in this claim.

effect_name: Familiarity fillers improve concealed memory detection
effect_claim: Adding familiarity-related filler items to a response-time concealed information test improves its ability to detect concealed knowledge.
effect_claim_quote: validity of the single-probe protocol version can be substantially improved by including familiarity-related fillers
original_title: Familiarity-Related Fillers Improve the Validity of Reaction Time-Based Memory Detection
original_journal: Journal of Applied Research in Memory and Cognition
replication_title: Addressing selective attrition in the enhanced response time-based concealed information test: A within-subject replication
replication_target_quote: current experiment replicates the original one, but using a within-subject design
outcome_quote: there is a large enhancement even when selective attrition is prevented
review_note: Corrected software-tool machine original link. Later author paper explicitly cites Lukács, Kleinberg & Verschuere (2017), repeats the E-CIT versus S-CIT comparison within participants to remove the selective attrition concern, and finds a large enhancement. The 2017 paper contained its own two internal studies; 2021 is a separate later experiment, albeit with shared first author.

effect_name: Higher childhood socioeconomic status predicts greater dispositional greed
effect_claim: Adolescents who grew up with higher socioeconomic status report more dispositional greed, especially only children.
effect_claim_quote: CSES was positively correlated with dispositional greed, and the moderating effect of family size was significant.
original_title: Scarcity or luxury: Which leads to adolescent greed? Evidence from a large-scale Chinese adolescent sample
original_authors: Liu Z, Sun X, Tsydypov L.
replication_title: Further tests of the scarcity and luxury hypotheses in dispositional greed: Evidence from two large-scale Dutch and American samples
replication_target_quote: We replicated this research in two other cultural contexts
outcome_quote: CSES was positively related to greed in both studies
review_note: Corrected original from unrelated DOI to Liu et al. 2019. Dutch and US samples both reproduce the positive childhood-status association. The sibling interaction appeared in only one of the two later studies, so this row codes the narrower main association only.

effect_name: Gender differences occur across Big Five personality aspects
effect_claim: Gender differences appear across the ten aspects beneath the Big Five personality domains.
effect_claim_quote: significant gender differences appearing in both aspects of every Big Five trait
original_title: Gender Differences in Personality across the Ten Aspects of the Big Five
original_authors: Weisberg YJ, Deyoung CG, Hirsh JB.
replication_title: Revisiting gender differences in 10 aspects of personality
replication_target_quote: This study aimed to replicate and extend the work of Weisberg et al. (2011)
outcome_quote: Overall, the results largely replicated Weisberg et al.'s findings, while also revealing meaningful contextual variations
review_note: Corrected original to Weisberg et al. 2011, not the machine-linked personality paper. Brazilian replication supports many aspect-level differences but reports cross-cultural divergences and age/education moderation; mixed for the all-aspect pattern.

effect_name: A general psychopathology factor explains comorbidity across disorders
effect_claim: A shared general psychopathology factor helps explain the structure of multiple psychiatric disorders beyond narrower symptom groups.
effect_claim_quote: Psychiatric disorders were initially explained by three higher-order factors (Internalizing, Externalizing, and Thought Disorder) but explained even better with one General Psychopathology dimension.
original_title: The p Factor: One General Psychopathology Factor in the Structure of Psychiatric Disorders?
original_authors: Caspi A, Houts RM, Belsky DW, Goldman-Mellor SJ, Harrington H, Israel S, Meier MH, Ramrakha S, Shalev I, Poulton R, Moffitt TE.
replication_title: The Structure of Psychopathology in Adolescence
replication_target_quote: This study aimed to replicate a study by Caspi and colleagues
outcome_quote: the structure of psychopathology is best characterized by a model including a general factor, in addition to smaller internalizing and externalizing factors
review_note: Corrected original to Caspi et al. 2014. Later adolescent self/parent data support a general factor alongside narrower internalizing and externalizing factors; conceptual replication with different age/sample measures.

effect_name: Positive affect and trait anger predict perceived workplace incivility
effect_claim: Positive affect and trait anger are the strongest personality predictors of how uncivil people perceive ambiguous workplace behavior to be.
effect_claim_quote: PA and trait anger explained the most variance in incivility perceptions
original_title: It Happened, or You Thought It Happened? Examining the Perception of Workplace Incivility Based on Personality Characteristics
replication_target_quote: replicate the findings from Sliter, Withrow, and Jex (2015)
outcome_quote: In both replications, positive affect and trait anger were the strongest predictors
review_note: The later proceedings abstract explicitly names Sliter, Withrow, and Jex (2015) and reports two replications. The author-uploaded primary article abstract confirms the named original DOI and the same effect. Later abstract contains a grammatical omission after “workplace”; outcome quote stops before it. Psychology of workplace incivility is within scope.
replication_title: Replications Further Examining Workplace Incivility Perceptions based on Personality Characteristics

effect_name: Subliminal approach training reduces implicit racial prejudice
effect_claim: Subliminally training people to approach Black faces and avoid White faces reduces implicit racial prejudice on a race association test.
effect_claim_quote: there was lower implicit prejudice on the IAT after training in approaching Blacks and avoiding Whites
original_title: (Close) Distance Makes the Heart Grow Fonder: Improving Implicit Racial Attitudes and Interracial Interactions Through Approach Behaviors
original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
replication_target_quote: a direct replication of the study by Kawakami et al. (2007)
outcome_quote: failed to provide any evidence for effects of subliminal AA training on implicit or explicit evaluations
review_note: The later article explicitly names Kawakami et al. (2007) and calls one experiment a direct replication. Original author-uploaded fulltext Study 2 used masked Black/White faces and reported lower IAT bias; the later paper did not find a subliminal approach-avoidance effect. Original omnibus Study 2 p=.06, planned contrast p=.03; claim is tied to planned contrast.
replication_title: Failures to change stimulus evaluations by means of subliminal approach and avoidance training.
replication_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

effect_name: Memory of a pairing supports transfer of negative valence
effect_claim: Negative pairings reduce how pleasant a neutral item feels, with this transfer of valence depending on episodic memory for the pairing.
effect_claim_quote: transfer of valence is contingent on episodic memory
original_title: Transfer of negative valence in an episodic memory task
replication_target_quote: Palombo, D. J., Elizur, L., Tuen, Y. J., Te, A. A., & Madan, C. R. (2021)
outcome_quote: We successfully replicated the EC effect and did not find an association between EC and episodic memory
review_note: The later Cognition & Emotion abstract explicitly cites the complete Palombo et al. (2021) original identity and tests single-trial evaluative conditioning in a VR paradigm. It reproduced the valence-transfer effect but not its association with episodic memory. This row is scoped to the memory-dependence component and labels the overall outcome mixed.
replication_title: Evaluative conditioning using virtual reality events

effect_name: Dehumanizing offenders predicts harsher punishment
effect_claim: Seeing criminal offenders as less human predicts harsher punishment, beyond differences in crime type, severity, and moral outrage.
effect_claim_quote: both moral outrage and dehumanization predicted punishment independently of the effects of crime type or crime severity
original_title: The Roles of Dehumanization and Moral Outrage in Retributive Justice
replication_target_quote: Previous work has reported that the extent to which participants dehumanized criminals
outcome_quote: apparent evidence for the relationship between trait-based dehumanization and punishment is better explained by the extent to which participants attribute socially desirable attributes to criminals
review_note: The later paper explicitly identifies Bastian, Denson, and Haslam (2013) in its fulltext and conceptually reproduces the original association in Studies 1A/1B. Its controlled and experimental studies attribute the apparent association to social desirability of traits rather than uniquely human traits. Mixed/qualified outcome reflects association reproduced but interpretation challenged. Original PLOS article and later Royal Society article are both primary fulltext.
replication_title: Attribution of undesirable character traits, rather than trait-based dehumanization, predicts punishment decisions
Religiosity and Support for Killing Animals: A Replication of the Curvilinear Relationship
effect_name: Moderate religiosity and lower support for killing animals
effect_claim: Support for killing animals was lower at moderate religiosity than at low or very high religiosity.
effect_claim_quote: The results indicated that, in support of our hypothesis, the relationship between religiosity and support for killing animals is curvilinear, as moderate levels of religiosity were related to less support for killing animals.
original_title: Religiosity and Support for Killing Animals: Evidence of a Curvilinear Relationship
replication_target_quote: Lifshin et al. (2018) theorized and found that this relationship may in fact be curvilinear, as moderate levels of religiosity relate to less support for killing animals compared to low religiosity (atheism) or to high religiosity (religious extremism or fundamentalism).
outcome_quote: Findings supported the hypothesis and suggest that moderate religiosity and belief in God are associated with less negative attitudes toward animals than atheism and disbelief on the one hand, and religious extremism on the other.
